name: Rome 98-117 AD
GovernmentType: Principate (De facto Autocracy / De jure Republic)
description: From 97 to 117 AD, Rome under Emperor Trajan reached the height of its power and territory. Expansion was achieved mainly through successful military campaigns, especially the Dacian Wars, which brought great wealth and secure borders along the Danube. Trajan also conquered parts of the Near East, including Armenia and Mesopotamia. Rome reached its maximum territorial extent in 117 AD, just before Trajan’s death.

name: Kingdom of Odoacer 476–493 AD
GovernmentType: Germanic kingship over Roman administrative structures
description: After the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476 AD, Odoacer ruled Italy as king. He maintained Roman institutions while exercising Germanic military power, governing until his defeat by Theodoric the Great in 493.

name: Ostrogothic Kingdom 493–534 AD
description: Founded by Theodoric the Great in 493 AD, the Ostrogothic Kingdom ruled Italy while preserving Roman law and institutions. It combined Gothic military leadership with Roman administration until its destruction during Justinian’s Gothic War.

name: Duchy of Modena and Reggio 1452–1859 AD
era: Late Medieval and Early Modern Italy
description: The Duchy of Modena and Reggio was established in 1452 when Borso d’Este was granted the ducal title by the Holy Roman Emperor. Ruled by the House of Este, it was a sovereign state within the Holy Roman Empire, known for its political stability, patronage of the arts, and strategic position in northern Italy. The duchy survived until 1859, when it was annexed during the Italian unification process.

name: Duchy of Parma and Piacenza 1545–1860 AD
description: The Duchy of Parma and Piacenza was created in 1545 by Pope Paul III for his son Pier Luigi Farnese. Ruled by the Farnese and later the Bourbons, it remained independent until annexed in 1859 during the Italian unification.

name: March of Verona (c. 951–1164 AD)
description: The March of Verona was established in the mid-10th century as a frontier territory of the Holy Roman Empire to control northeastern Italy. It declined as imperial authority weakened and was absorbed by autonomous communes and local lordships by the 12th century.

name: Duchy of Milan 1395–1545 AD
era: Late Medieval and Early Modern Italy
GovernmentType: Hereditary duchy (Visconti, Sforza, later Habsburg rule)
description: The Duchy of Milan was created in 1395 when Emperor Wenceslaus granted ducal status to Gian Galeazzo Visconti. A major power in northern Italy, it later passed to the Sforza and then to foreign dynasties, ending with Napoleon’s conquest in 1796.

name: Duchy of Milan (1545–1796 AD)
currency: Milanese lira, Spanish and Imperial coinage
GovernmentType: Imperial duchy under Spanish and Austrian Habsburg rule
description: After 1545, the Duchy of Milan lost Parma and Piacenza and became a Habsburg-controlled state. Ruled first by Spain and later by Austria, it remained an important strategic territory in northern Italy until its dissolution by Napoleon in 1796.

name: Republic of Venice 700-1095 AD
description: From 700 to 1095, the Republic of Venice evolved from a Byzantine dependency into a powerful maritime republic, expanding trade networks, securing independence, developing institutions, and emerging as a dominant Mediterranean commercial and naval force.

name: Republic of Venice 1430-1570 AD
description: From 1430 to 1570, the Republic of Venice reached its zenith, dominating Mediterranean trade, flourishing in art and architecture, facing Ottoman expansion, losing eastern territories, yet remaining a powerful, wealthy, and culturally vibrant state.

name: Republica di Amalfi 839 AD - 1137 AD
description: The Republic of Amalfi, a maritime power in southern Italy (9th–11th centuries), dominated Mediterranean trade, developed early banking and naval innovations, and maintained independence until Norman conquest integrated it into the Kingdom of Sicily.

name: Republica di Ancona 1000-1532 AD
description: The Republic of Ancona, a small maritime republic on Italy’s Adriatic coast (11th–16th centuries), thrived on trade and shipbuilding, maintaining political autonomy while navigating pressures from Venice, the Papal States, and other regional powers.

name: Republica di Noli 1192-1797 AD
description: The Republic of Noli, a tiny maritime republic in Liguria, Italy (12th–18th centuries), maintained independence through alliances with Genoa, focused on trade and local defense, and was eventually absorbed into the Ligurian Republic under Napoleon.

name: Republica di Genoa 1005 AD
description: The Republic of Genoa was a maritime republic from 1099 to 1797, controlling major trade routes in the Mediterranean and Black Seas. It was a powerful commercial and financial center, a rival to Venice, and had a vast network of colonies and trading posts.

name: Republic of Genoa 1566-1755 AD
description: The Republic of Genoa was a maritime republic from 1099 to 1797, controlling major trade routes in the Mediterranean and Black Seas. It was a powerful commercial and financial center, a rival to Venice, and had a vast network of colonies and trading posts.

name: Duchy of Gaeta 839-1140 AD
description: The Duchy of Gaeta was a small but strategically important maritime state in southern Italy during the Early Middle Ages. Originally under Byzantine influence, it became effectively independent in the 9th century. Ruled by local dynasties, it balanced diplomacy between Byzantines, Lombards, and Muslims before being absorbed by the Normans in the 12th century.

name: Duchy of Savoy 1416-1770
GovernmentType: Initially a duchy, later hereditary monarchy.
description: The Duchy of Savoy was created in 1416 when Emperor Sigismund of the Holy Roman Empire elevated the County of Savoy to ducal rank. The ruling House of Savoy gradually expanded its territory on both sides of the Alps, controlling strategic Alpine passes between France and Italy. Over time, the political center shifted eastward, and Turin became the capital, marking a stronger Italian orientation.

name: Duchy of Mantua 1530-1708
GovernmentType: Initially a marquisate, later a hereditary duchy.
description: The Duchy of Mantua was created in 1530 when Emperor Charles V elevated the Marquisate of Mantua to ducal rank under the Gonzaga family. Mantua had previously been ruled as a marquisate since 1433. The Gonzaga transformed the city into a major cultural center of the Italian Renaissance. The duchy remained a hereditary state within the Holy Roman Empire until 1708, when it was abolished after the War of the Spanish Succession and annexed by the Habsburg Monarchy.

name: Duchy of Ferrara 1471-1598
GovernmentType: Initially a marquisate, later a hereditary duchy.
description: The Duchy of Ferrara was established in 1471 when Pope Paul II elevated the Marquisate of Ferrara to ducal status under the House of Este. Previously ruled as a marquisate, Ferrara became a prominent Renaissance court and cultural center. The duchy remained a hereditary state until 1598, when it reverted to direct Papal control following the extinction of the legitimate Este line.

name: Duchy of Urbino 1443-1631
GovernmentType: Initially a county, later a hereditary duchy.
description: The Duchy of Urbino was created in 1443 when Pope Eugene IV elevated the County of Urbino to ducal rank under the Montefeltro family. Renowned as a leading Renaissance court, Urbino flourished as a center of art, humanism, and military leadership. The duchy remained a hereditary state until 1631, when it was absorbed into the Papal States following the extinction of the ruling dynasty.

name: Republic of Florence 1115-1406 AD
description: The Republic of Florence was a powerful city-state in Tuscany, governed by merchant oligarchs and later the Medici, known for banking wealth, republican institutions, and extraordinary cultural influence during the Renaissance.

name: kingdom of Naples 1282-1806 & 1815-1816 AD
description: The Kingdom of Naples, officially the Kingdom of Sicily, was a state that ruled the part of the Italian Peninsula south of the Papal States between 1282 and 1816.

name: Republic of Siena 1125 AD
description: The Republic of Siena (1125–1555) was an Italian city-state, governed as an oligarchic republic, with an economy based on banking and trade, renowned for its art, culture, and Gothic architecture.

name: Republic of Lucca 1160-1805 AD
description: The Republic of Lucca was a small independent state in Tuscany, thriving as a banking and silk center. Governed by oligarchic institutions, it preserved its autonomy until annexed by Napoleon in 1805.

name: Kingdom of Sicily 1282-1806 AD
description: In 1282, the Kingdom of Sicily erupted during the Sicilian Vespers, expelling Angevin rule. It transformed into a vibrant Mediterranean power, blending Norman, Arab, and Byzantine influences under Aragonese protection and enduring legacy.

description: The Republic of San Marino, annexation of Serravalle, Faetano and Montegiardino. Since then its territory remains unchanged.

name: Papal States 1600-1859
description: The Papal States were a conglomeration of territories on the Italian peninsula under the direct sovereign rule of the pope from 756 to 1870. They were among the major states of Italy from the 8th century until the unification of Italy, which took place between 1859 and 1870, culminating in their demise.

name: Papal States 1859-1870 AD
description: Papal states after losing some territory to the unification of Italy.

name: Vatican city 1929AD-today
description: Vatican City is the smallest sovereign state in the world, an enclave within Rome ruled by the Pope as the head of the Catholic Church. Established in 1929, it is the center of the Catholic world, home to significant sites like St. Peter's Basilica and the Vatican Museums.

name: Italy 1960-Present
description: In 1960 Italy ended its last colonial administration when the Trust Territory of Somalia gained independence, concluding its postwar decolonization. After losing its African empire following World War II, Italy focused on economic growth, becoming a founding member of the European Economic Community. Despite political instability and economic challenges, it developed as a parliamentary republic and remains a key member of the European Union.

name: Malta 1964-Present
description: Malta gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1964, initially remaining a constitutional monarchy within the Commonwealth. In 1974 it became a republic. British forces withdrew in 1979, marking full sovereignty. Malta later pursued neutrality and economic modernization, joining the European Union in 2004 and adopting the euro in 2008. Today it is a parliamentary republic and an active EU member in the Mediterranean region.

name: Sovereign Rule of the Order of St. John in Malta 1551-1798 AD
description: In 1530 Charles V granted Malta and Tripoli to the Order of St. John after their expulsion from Rhodes. Tripoli was lost to the Ottomans in 1551, but Malta remained their stronghold, notably resisting the Great Siege of 1565. The Order ruled as a sovereign military and religious state until 1798, when Napoleon Bonaparte seized Malta during his expedition to Egypt, ending Hospitaller rule.

name: Sovereign Rule of the Order of St. John in Malta 1530-1551 AD
description: In 1530 Charles V granted Malta and Tripoli to the Order of St. John after their expulsion from Rhodes. The Knights established their base in Birgu and governed as a sovereign military-religious state. Tripoli, poorly defended and isolated, was captured by Ottoman forces in 1551, marking the Order’s loss of its North African possession while Malta remained under their control.
